chunks: Overcurrent load on a long supply trace.
The question: What happens if your load tries to draw too much current but there's lots of trace distance between your load and power supply?
When a load pulls too much current through a long, thin supply trace, several things happen at once. The voltage at the load sags, because the trace has resistance.
The trace heats up and can be damaged. The supply may clamp, back off or restart repeatedly. And the regulator does not notice the sag, because it senses its own output.
The cure is copper sized for the fault, protection at the source, and a clean undervoltage reset at the load.
Picture a long garden hose feeding a sprinkler. If the sprinkler suddenly demands far more water, the hose loses pressure, so the sprinkler fades.
The hose also strains and can burst if the pump pushes too hard. The pump's gauge, at the near end of the hose, still reads full pressure, so it never knows.
A relief valve at the pump, set below what the hose can take, is the protection.
With a 100 milliohms path the curve ends at 27 watts: the square root turns imaginary, which means there is no stable operating point and the rail collapses.
Even before that, the load drops below a 10% tolerance (2. 97 volts) at about 10 watts. A 20 milliohms path only reaches the 10% limit at about 50 watts.
Brown-out: the supply falls below the load's minimum, causing resets or errors.
IR drop and I to the 2R : the voltage lost and the heat made in the trace ("High-current layout rules of thumb").
Current limit modes: constant current, foldback (limit falls as voltage falls), hiccup (shut down and retry), latch-off.
Constant-power load: a load like a converter whose current rises as its voltage falls ("Why the supply goes close to the load").
UVLO: undervoltage lockout, which holds the load off below a threshold.
A 1 mm wide, 1 oz trace is 50 mm long. That is 50 squares, or 24 milliohms one way. At 10 amps, each path drops 10 times 0. 024 equals 0.
24 volts and dissipates 10 squared times 0. 024 equals 2. 4 watts in a tiny strip of copper. The IPC chart rates that trace at only about 3. 2 amps for a 20 degrees Celsius rise.
So the load browns out, the trace overheats, and the regulator does not see either. That is the whole idea.
"The voltage at the load sags by current times trace resistance, because the regulator senses locally and can't compensate, so the load may brown out.
The trace dissipates I to the 2R and can overheat, damage the board or fuse: 1 mm of 1 oz copper fuses around 10 amps in a second.
The supply may hit current limit, fold back or hiccup, and a constant-power load can collapse.
The fix is copper sized for fault current, a fuse or limit at the source, remote sense, and a clean UVLO."
